messages:
alex: Ran a perf record + FlameGraph on staging for the new batching scheduler. Seeing surprising CPU time in Python land — largely in tokenization and PyEval frames. attaching quick notes and a tiny flame snippet from perf.svg :eyes:

mira: ugh, that sounds like the GIL fighting us. can you paste the perf command you ran?

alex: Ran:```bash
sudo perf record -F 99 -g -p $(pgrep -f redwood-runtime) -- sleep 60
perf script | ./stackcollapse-perf.pl > out.folded
./flamegraph.pl out.folded > perf.svg
```
Got a big block labeled `tokenize.py:split` and `PyEval_EvalFrameEx` with lots of C->Python transitions.

ben: Two quick asks: 1) is the runtime single-threaded on CPU side (the scheduler loop)? 2) any recent changes to tokenization lib (regex -> new wordpiece)?

alex: 1) scheduler thread is single-threaded for batch assembly, but worker threads handle model IO. 2) yes we swapped to fastwordpiece v2 last week. I thought it sped things up though.

mira: fastwordpiece tends to allocate more small objects. perf flame can hide allocator time as Python frames. try sampling with py-spy (no sudo) to confirm Python-level hotspots:```bash
py-spy record -o pyspy.svg --native --pid $(pgrep -f redwood-runtime) --duration 60
```
py-spy will show Python stacks and native frames.

alex: did py-spy; pyspy.svg indeed shows heavy `Tokenization._split_on_whitespace` and also a surprising `Scheduler.tick` C-extension wrapper calling back into Python for metric callbacks.

ben: metric callbacks — we add a synchronous call to `emit_metric()` in the hot path, right? that can be constant overhead. consider deferring to async queue.

sylvia: FYI I reproduced locally with perf and saw syscalls spike (~open/close) — maybe tokenization touches disk for vocab lookup fallback?

alex: good catch. i'll grep for any `open(` in tokenizer code. Found a fallback that loads `vocab.json` if lookup misses. But it should be cached; might be a bug on cold-start path.

mira: if it's cached at module level, but we recreate Tokenizer per request, you'll hit disk repeatedly. keep one shared vocab or use lru cache.

alex: patched local branch to hoist vocab loading into a singleton. Re-ran perf; flamegraph main python blocks reduced ~30%. Still seeing `Scheduler._assemble_batches` CPU in Python.

ben: share the flame subset? also try `perf top -p PID` while running a high-RPS synthetic to see realtime hot functions. perf top helps when scripts obscure short-lived frames.

alex: uploaded perf snippets to gist: https://gist.github.com/rw/perf-token-sched (notes in gist). Perf top confirms `PyObject_Call` heavy and `PyEval_EvalFrameEx`.

mira: two more experiments: 1) run with `PYTHONMALLOC=malloc` to see if small object allocator is contributing; 2) run with compiled C tokenization (we have a draft C extension) to compare.

alex: did PYTHONMALLOC test — marginal improvement (~8%). C extension test: tokenization CPU dropped ~60%, but scheduling still consumes ~18% in Python due to `should_flush_batch()` checks and per-token logging.

ben: sounds like batching decision logic is hot. Can you paste the loop? maybe we can vectorize checks or move to C.

alex: loop is short:```python
while cur_batch_size < max_batch and queue:
    req = queue.popleft()
    if not should_keep(req):
        continue
    batch.append(req)
    if req.priority: maybe_promote(batch)
```
`should_keep` does a few regexp checks and a small token-length calc.

mira: regexp in hot path = bad. Precompute boolean flags when enqueuing or push simple heuristics into routing (C++ side) so scheduler only sees O(1) checks.

sylvia: also consider moving `maybe_promote` to a separate pass after initial gather; promotions cause branching and cache churn.

alex: moving some logic off the scheduler thread to enqueuer helped — CPU on scheduler thread dropped another ~20%. End-to-end latency improved ~12% p50 under load.

perf-bot: automated note: attached perf artifacts: perf.raw (60s), pyspy.svg, perf.svg. Upload URL: https://artifacts.internal/redwood/perf/1761234567/

ben: nice. remaining work: 1) land C tokenization, 2) move should_keep to enqueuer, 3) async metrics + batch logging. Also add unit perf tests that run `perf record` with the synthetic workload.

mira: add flame regression test to CI: record baseline flame and ensure new runs don't add >5% Python CPU in `Scheduler` frame. Could be noisy but worth a try on dedicated perf runners.

alex: will open PRs for the three items and a follow-up thread once CI runs are in. thanks all. :rocket:
